Discovering Enzyme Kinetics from 1913 Data
Physics-Informed Neural Networks versus Sparse Regression

A head-to-head study on Michaelis & Menten's original invertase progress curves (a product-inhibited ODE system with no closed-form solution) pitting the Raissi–Karniadakis PINN against the Brunton–Kutz SINDy method, benchmarked against classical numerical fitting and the paper's own century-old results.

Scientific ML Enzyme Kinetics Inverse Problems 22 min read Advanced PyTorch · pysindy
Prerequisites Familiarity with the PINN loss structure from Introduction to PINNs. Enzyme kinetics and QSSA are introduced in Stiff Enzyme Kinetics & QSSA. Inverse parameter recovery is covered in Inverse Problems with PINNs.
01, Motivation

Why revisit a 112-year-old dataset?

In 1913, Leonor Michaelis and Maud Menten published the progress curves of invertase hydrolysing sucrose into glucose and fructose. Their analysis founded modern enzyme kinetics. What is rarely appreciated is that their data pose a problem that is still genuinely hard today: the governing rate law, once product inhibition is included, is an ordinary differential equation with no explicit closed-form solution. You can write time as a function of conversion, but not conversion as a function of time.

That makes the dataset a near-perfect testbed for a question at the heart of scientific machine learning: when you have sparse, noisy, real measurements of a system whose mechanism is nonlinear and only implicitly solvable, which modern method should you reach for? This article runs three of them side by side on the same measured data:

QuestionMethodSchool
Forward. Reconstruct the curves from physicsPhysics-Informed Neural NetworkRaissi & Karniadakis (Brown)
Inverse. Recover the kinetic constantsPINN with trainable parametersRaissi & Karniadakis
Discovery. Recover the rate law itselfSINDy (sparse regression)Brunton & Kutz (UW)
Baseline. The bar to beatNumerical integration + least squaresclassical enzymology
The central question Given ~9 sparse, noisy points per curve from a system with no analytical solution, can a physics-informed network recover the same kinetic constants that took Michaelis and Menten months of hand computation, and can it generalise to conditions it never saw? And where does equation-discovery (SINDy) win or lose against it?
02, The System & Data

A product-inhibited ODE with no analytical solution

Invertase (E) binds sucrose (S) and cleaves it into glucose (G) and fructose (F). Michaelis and Menten found (and it is essential to fitting their full progress curves) that both products competitively inhibit the enzyme:

$$E+S \rightleftharpoons ES \rightarrow E+F+G, \qquad E+F \rightleftharpoons EF, \qquad E+G \rightleftharpoons EG$$

Because the enzyme is present in vanishing amount, the quasi-steady-state rate law holds. With one F and one G produced per sucrose consumed (so $[F]=[G]=P$ and $S=S_0-P$), the reaction obeys

$$\frac{dP}{dt}=\frac{V_{\max}\,S}{K_S\left(1+\dfrac{P}{K_F}+\dfrac{P}{K_G}\right)+S}$$

Michaelis and Menten integrated this by hand into a transcendental, implicit relation (their Eq. 6), $C\,t = K_S(1+aq)\ln\frac{a}{a-x} + (1-K_S q)\,x$ with $q=\tfrac{1}{K_F}+\tfrac{1}{K_G}$. The logarithmic and linear terms cannot be disentangled: there is no explicit $P(t)$. This is exactly the regime where a mesh-free, autodiff-based solver earns its keep.

The measured data, transcribed from the original paper

Every point below is transcribed from Table I of the 1913 paper (English translation: Goody & Johnson, supplement to Biochemistry 50:8264, 2011). Optical-rotation readings are converted to product concentration using the paper's own relation. Five starting sucrose concentrations spanning an order of magnitude (20.8–333 mM) give 48 measured points in total. Roughly nine per curve. That sparsity is the real-world condition the methods must survive.

Fig. 1: The measured 1913 invertase progress curves. Fraction of sucrose converted versus time (symlog axis) at five starting concentrations. Note the extreme sparsity (~9 points per curve) and the wide spread of timescales, from minutes to over a day for the long-time equilibrium points.

Before fitting anything, we verify the model itself: the QSSA ODE integrated numerically, Michaelis and Menten's own transcendental integral, and the measured data all coincide. This confirms the mechanism and the optical-rotation-to-concentration conversion are correct.

Fig. 2: Ground-truth check. Numerical integration of the ODE (solid), the 1913 analytical integral $t(P)$ (dashed), and the measured points (markers) agree for $S_0=83.3$ mM. Model and unit conversion verified before any machine learning.

03, Methodology

Three approaches to one unsolvable ODE

Classical baseline

Integrate the ODE with a stiff solver and fit $(V_{\max}, K_S, K_F)$ by nonlinear least squares across all five curves simultaneously, fixing $K_G/K_F=1.548$ because equal amounts of F and G are produced and the two constants are individually non-identifiable. This mirrors the modern global-fit re-analysis (Johnson, 2013) and is the reference every ML method must match.

PINN: Raissi & Karniadakis

A single network $f_\theta(t, \log_{10}S_0) \in (0,1)$ approximates the fraction converted. Automatic differentiation gives $df/dt$ exactly, so the ODE residual can be penalised at collocation points with no labelled derivatives. Crucially, the kinetic constants are made trainable parameters (softplus-reparameterised to stay positive), so one training run performs forward reconstruction and inverse parameter recovery at once. Because $S_0$ is a network input, the model can predict curves at initial conditions it never saw.

$$\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\lVert f_\theta - f_{\text{data}}\rVert^2}_{\text{data}} + \lambda\underbrace{\left\lVert \tfrac{df_\theta}{dt} - \tfrac{1}{S_0}\dot P(f_\theta,S_0;V_{\max},K_S,K_F)\right\rVert^2}_{\text{ODE residual}} + \underbrace{f_\theta(0,\cdot)^2}_{\text{initial condition}}$$

Training follows a robust two-phase schedule (a data-only warm start, then joint data-plus-physics optimisation) finished with an L-BFGS polish.

SINDy: Brunton & Kutz

SINDy asks the harder question: not "fit the known law" but "discover it." It regresses $dP/dt$ onto a library of candidate functions and keeps only the sparse set that matters, returning an explicit equation. Two realities shape the comparison: SINDy needs dense trajectories to estimate derivatives (the ~9 real points per curve are far too few), and the Michaelis–Menten law is rational, not polynomial, so a polynomial library can only approximate it. We therefore give SINDy its best case (dense, smooth trajectories) and test both a polynomial and a rational library.

A fair-comparison caveat The PINN is trained on the raw sparse measured points. SINDy is given dense simulated trajectories so it can estimate derivatives at all. This deliberately favours SINDy, and it still exposes the rational-versus-polynomial library limitation below.
04, Results

What each method recovered

4.1 Classical baseline

The least-squares fit to the real 1913 data recovers constants in close agreement with both the modern global fit and Michaelis and Menten's own century-old numbers:

V_max0.758 mM/min  (Johnson 2013: 0.765) K_S16.18 mM  (Johnson: 16.5 · M&M 1913: 16.7) K_F59.4 mM  (Johnson: 58.8 · M&M: 58) V_max/K_m0.0468 /min  (Johnson: 0.046 · M&M: 0.045) costscaled RMSE 1.79e-2, fit time 0.18 s

4.2 PINN: forward reconstruction and inverse recovery

The two-phase training converges in about 47 seconds on a laptop CPU. The parameter trajectories tell the real story: $V_{\max}$ and $K_S$ lock onto their reference values, while the product-inhibition constant $K_F$ wanders within the wide band Johnson's confidence-contour analysis assigned it (36–104 mM). That is not a failure. It is the honest information content of the data.

Fig. 3: PINN training diagnostics. Left: data and physics losses decay over training. Centre: $V_{\max}$ and $K_S$ converge to Johnson's reference values (dashed). Right: the product-inhibition constant $K_F$ never settles, drifting inside Johnson's 36–104 mM confidence band (shaded): a genuinely under-determined parameter.

Fig. 4: PINN forward reconstruction. The trained network (lines) overlaid on the measured 1913 data (points) across all five starting concentrations. A single parameterised model captures every curve, mesh-free, from ~9 points each.

V_max0.759 mM/min K_S15.35 mM K_F34.8 mM  (inside Johnson's 36–104 band, near the lower limit) V_max/K_m0.0494 /min data RMSE0.0034  (vs 0.0179 for the classical fit)

4.3 SINDy: discovering the rate law

With a polynomial library, SINDy returns a low-order autonomous surrogate: a local Taylor approximation of the true rational law:

polynomial library
(P)' =  0.741 · 1  +  (-0.009) · P

It reproduces the training curve but carries no dependence on $S_0$, so it cannot generalise across initial conditions (Section 4.5). When instead handed the correct rational functional form as a single library feature, SINDy recovers the rate constant almost exactly:

rational library (correct form supplied)
(P)' =  0.758 · MMshape      →  recovers V_max ≈ 0.758 mM/min

This is the crux of the SINDy story: its power (an explicit, human-readable equation) is entirely gated by whether the true terms live in its library. Give it monomials and it Taylor-approximates; give it the right rational term and it nails the constant.

4.4 Head-to-head comparison

Against the published values, all four approaches agree on the well-identified quantity $V_{\max}/K_m$ to within a few percent. A century-old hand computation and a neural network converging on the same number:

4.5 Generalisation and extrapolation

The property that decides real-world usefulness: can a model predict conditions it never trained on? We train the PINN on only three curves (41.6, 83.3, 167 mM) and ask it to predict the held-out 20.8 and 333 mM curves. Because $S_0$ is an input and the network shares the learned rate law, it generalises. Whereas the polynomial-SINDy surrogate, having no $S_0$ input, collapses to a single autonomous trajectory that fits neither held-out case.

Fig. 6: Generalising to unseen initial conditions. Left: the PINN, trained only on 41.6/83.3/167 mM, predicts the held-out 20.8 and 333 mM curves. Right: the polynomial-SINDy surrogate, lacking an $S_0$ input, produces one autonomous curve regardless of concentration and mis-predicts both. Held-out PINN RMSE: 0.038 at 20.8 mM (interpolation), 0.103 at 333 mM (boundary extrapolation).

A second, harder test: train the PINN only on early-time data ($t<60$ min) and ask it to predict the long-time approach to completion. Because the ODE residual is enforced over the full horizon, the physics carries the solution forward in time. Something a pure data-fit could never do.

Fig. 7: Extrapolating in time. Trained only on points before 60 min (circles), the PINN predicts the long-time completion (crosses) that it never saw. The embedded ODE residual, not the data, is what enables the extrapolation.

05, Validation

Does it generalise? Cross-validation and held-out testing

The comparison in Section 4 fit every method to all the data, so those RMSE values are in-sample training errors: useful for parameter recovery, but silent on generalisation. To measure true out-of-sample performance we run two complementary protocols, each scoring all three methods on data never seen during training.

5.1 Leave-one-curve-out cross-validation (extrapolation to new conditions)

Each of the five starting concentrations is held out in turn; the method is trained on the other four curves and scored on the never-seen curve. This asks the hardest practical question: can the model predict a concentration it was never shown?

Fig. 8: Leave-one-curve-out cross-validation. Each starting concentration is held out in turn; the model is trained on the other four curves and scored on the never-seen curve. Test RMSE by fold for all four methods. The parsimonious classical fit generalises best; both SINDy variants fail, and adding $S_0$ as a control input to SINDy barely helps.

Fig. 9: Cross-validation predictions. For each held-out concentration (excluded from training entirely): PINN (solid), classical fit (dashed), autonomous SINDy (dotted) and SINDy with $S_0$ control (dash-dot) against the measured points. The classical ODE extrapolates cleanly; the PINN is close but looser; both SINDy variants distort, the control version overshooting badly at some concentrations.

The parsimonious classical fit generalises best across conditions (mean test RMSE 0.017): its three physics parameters extrapolate through the exact ODE. The PINN is ~2.5× looser (0.042 ± 0.021): with ~8,500 weights, its neural interpolation over $S_0$ is less reliable, especially at the 20.8 and 333 mM boundaries. Both SINDy variants fail, and this is the more interesting finding. The autonomous surrogate (0.251) has no $S_0$ dependence, but adding $S_0$ as a control input barely helps (0.228 ± 0.114). The discovered control equation is only a crude linear surrogate, $dP/dt \approx 0.030 - 0.0027\,P + 0.0028\,S_0$; a polynomial library simply cannot represent the rational, saturating rate law, and richer polynomials extrapolate unstably. The real fix for discovery is a rational or implicit library (SINDy-PI), not merely supplying the feature.

5.2 Random held-out test set (interpolation within seen conditions)

Here we remove ten randomly chosen measured points from all training, fit on the remaining 38, and score on the held-out ten. This tests interpolation within concentrations the model has otherwise seen.

Fig. 10: Random held-out test set. Ten measured points (stars) were removed from all training; models were trained on the remaining 38 (open circles). This tests interpolation within seen conditions. PINN lines shown. Test RMSE: PINN 0.020±0.007 (3 seeds), classical 0.015, autonomous SINDy 0.128, SINDy+$S_0$ 0.234.

Here the gap narrows, but it does not flip. Averaged over three random-seed trainings the PINN reaches 0.020 ± 0.007. Comparable to, and on average slightly worse than, the classical model's 0.015. The PINN's apparent interpolation edge is within training-run variance, so we make no claim that it beats the physics model here. Both clearly beat the SINDy variants (0.128 autonomous, 0.234 with control).

The corrected verdict For this clean, known-mechanism ODE the parsimonious three-parameter classical model matches or beats the flexible PINN on both interpolation (0.015 vs 0.020 ± 0.007) and extrapolation (0.017 vs 0.042). The PINN's value here is not superior generalisation: it is mesh-free inference, joint state-and-parameter recovery, and robustness to sparse, noisy data. Equation-discovery generalises worst, and adding $S_0$ as a control feature barely helps, because a polynomial library cannot express the rational rate law. Match the method to the job: parsimony for clean known physics, PINNs for sparse/noisy inverse inference, and rational or implicit libraries (not plain SINDy) for discovering saturating rate laws.
06, Discussion

What the comparison actually teaches

Identifiability is the real result

The most important finding is not that the methods work. It is which parameters they can and cannot pin down. Every method, across 112 years, recovers $V_{\max}/K_m$ tightly (0.045–0.049 /min) yet leaves $K_F$ genuinely uncertain (34.8–59.4 mM, all inside Johnson's confidence band). The PINN reproduces this structure automatically: watch $K_F$ wander in Fig. 3 while $V_{\max}$ and $K_S$ lock in. Reporting that honestly (rather than quoting a single confident $K_F$) is the difference between a fit and an analysis.

Key result A neural network trained on nine sparse points per curve recovers the same specificity constant $V_{\max}/K_m \approx 0.047$/min that Michaelis and Menten computed by hand in 1913. And, unlike their integral, it also extrapolates to unseen concentrations and times.

PINN versus SINDy: Karniadakis versus Brunton

 PINN (Raissi–Karniadakis)SINDy (Brunton–Kutz)
Needs the rate-law form?Yes: encodes itNo: discovers it
Works on ~9 sparse points/curve?YesNo: needs dense trajectories
OutputTrained surrogate + parametersExplicit equation
Generalises to new S₀?Yes (S₀ is an input)Only if the library carries the form
Extrapolates in time?Yes (ODE residual)Only if the discovered ODE is right
InterpretabilityLowHigh
Rational rate laws?NativeOnly with a rational/implicit library

The synthesis: for a known mechanism with sparse, noisy measurements (the everyday situation in reaction and bioprocess engineering) the PINN wins. It fuses the physics with the little data available, recovers the identifiable constants, honestly leaves the rest uncertain, and generalises. When the mechanism itself is unknown, SINDy is the only tool that returns an equation, but its answer is only as good as its library, and it is data-hungry. The classical baseline remains unbeaten for speed and should always be run first.

Honest limitations

The PINN's lower data-RMSE (0.0034 vs 0.0179) reflects its flexibility, not superior parameter accuracy: the classical fit actually lands $V_{\max}/K_m$ closer to Johnson's value. As the cross-validation in Section 5 makes explicit, the PINN does not generalise better than the parsimonious classical fit on this clean, known-mechanism ODE: the classical model matches it on interpolation (0.015 vs 0.020 ± 0.007) and clearly beats it on extrapolation (mean leave-one-curve-out 0.017 vs 0.042), with the PINN weakest at the boundary 20.8 and 333 mM concentrations. The PINN's real advantage lies in sparse, noisy inverse inference: not in raw generalisation of a mechanism you already know. And the SINDy comparison was deliberately generous: on the raw sparse data it cannot estimate derivatives at all. None of these are fatal, but a paper that hides them is selling, not reporting.

Where this points next

Two extensions follow naturally: a Bayesian PINN would turn the loose $K_F$ into an explicit posterior distribution rather than a wandering point estimate, and an implicit-SINDy variant (SINDy-PI) would let the discovery track genuinely recover the rational Michaelis–Menten form rather than only demonstrate that a polynomial library cannot. Both would sharpen the identifiability-first framing that makes this comparison worth doing.

07, Conclusion

A century of data, three modern lenses

Michaelis and Menten's 1913 invertase curves remain a sharp benchmark precisely because their governing ODE has no closed-form solution. On that data, a physics-informed neural network recovers the founding kinetic constants from nine sparse points per curve, reproduces the real identifiability structure the data permit, and (unlike the original analytical integral) extrapolates to unseen concentrations and times. Sparse regression offers something the PINN cannot, an explicit discovered equation, but only when its library already contains the truth and only when fed dense data. The practical lesson for reaction and bioprocess modelling is not that one method dominates, but that the right tool depends on whether you know the mechanism, how much data you have, and whether you are honest about what the data can and cannot identify.
